text: George Alexander Porterfield (November 24, 1822 – February 27, 1919) was a junior officer in the United States Army during the Mexican–American War, served as a colonel in the Confederate States Army during the first year of the American Civil War, and later became a longtime banker in Charles Town, West Virginia. Born in Berkeley County, Virginia, he was the son of George and Mary (Tabb) Porterfield and grandson of William and Rachel (Vance) Porterfield; his grandfather was a Revolutionary War captain, justice of Berkeley County in 1785, and high sheriff in 1803, while his father was a War of 1812 veteran. Porterfield graduated from the Virginia Military Institute in 1844 and, in May 1846, helped organize the first company of Virginia volunteers for the Mexican–American War, becoming first lieutenant. He was later appointed adjutant of the 1st Virginia Regiment, acting assistant adjutant general of his brigade, and assistant adjutant general of the division at Buena Vista. After the war, he became an editor of the Martinsburg Gazette and a teacher, worked briefly for the United States Coast Survey in Washington, D.C., and returned to Jefferson County as a farmer in 1855. On July 9, 1849, he married Emily Cornelia Terrill, daughter of Elizabeth (Pitzer) Terrill and Colonel William Henry Terrill, a lawyer, prosecuting attorney, and member of the Virginia House of Delegates, who also served as provost marshal during the Civil War; she was sister to Confederate General James Barbour Terrill, Union General William Rufus Terrill, and Phillip M. Terrill, a lieutenant in the 12th Virginia Infantry, all of whom were killed in action, and to George Parker Terrill, who survived the war, served as a Confederate colonel, and later as a recruiter and post surgeon. Porterfield and Emily had four sons and three daughters; their son John followed in the banking business. After Virginia seceded on April 17, 1861, Governor John Letcher authorized the formation of state forces, appointing Robert E. Lee as major general to command them. Porterfield was initially appointed colonel and inspector general of militia at Harpers Ferry and then ordered by Lee on May 4, 1861, to organize forces at Grafton, northwest Virginia, to protect the main line and Parkersburg branch of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. He arrived in Grafton on May 14, 1861, found the town mostly pro-Union with the Grafton Guards militia already in Union service, and established a base at Fetterman, about 2 miles north. There, he found Capt. William P. Thompson and his Marion Guards equipped with 175 muskets. He reported to Lee that companies were being raised in Clarksburg, Pruntytown, Philippi, Weston, and Fairmont, but only two were armed, one with "old flint-lock muskets, in bad order, and no ammunition." The companies under his command were later organized into the 25th Virginia Infantry, the 31st Virginia Infantry, and the 9th Battalion of Virginia Infantry. He advised Richmond that a large force was needed to hold the area, but leaders including Lee refused to send troops from eastern Virginia due to concerns about provoking Union sympathizers. On May 19, Lee sent two companies from Staunton to Beverly under Porterfield’s command. After the Grafton Guards moved to Wheeling to join the Union Army, Porterfield occupied Grafton on May 25 but soon withdrew due to the threat of Union advances. He ordered Colonel William J. Willey to burn two bridges on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad between Farmington and Mannington on May 25. With only about 550 poorly equipped men, lacking arms and ammunition, and learning that Union forces under Major General George B. McClellan were advancing toward Grafton, Porterfield realized his position was untenable. Union forces under Colonel Benjamin Franklin Kelley and Colonel James B. Steedman were moving toward Grafton to protect the railroad. On May 28, Porterfield withdrew to Philippi, a strongly secessionist town about 30 miles south of Grafton. On May 30, Kelley occupied Grafton and repaired the bridges. Porterfield picked up two additional companies but had to send two back due to lack of arms and ammunition. A Confederate court of inquiry on July 4, 1861, concluded that Porterfield had 600 effective infantry and 175 cavalry at Philippi. On June 2, 1861, General Morris sent two columns—Kelley and Ebenezer Dumont—to attack Porterfield at Philippi. On June 3, 1861, at dawn, the larger Union force surprised the Confederate troops, who were mostly asleep, due to poor picket placement and premature firing. Some returned fire, but the entire force fled in disorder, leaving most supplies; only a few were wounded, including Union Colonel Kelley, and a small number of Confederates were captured. The battle was nicknamed the "Philippi Races." Porterfield and surviving men retreated to Beverly, about 30 miles south. He was blamed for the defeat and requested a court of inquiry, which concluded that pickets were on duty, most of his command left in good order, and he had planned to evacuate as soon as the attack was imminent. General Lee censured Porterfield for unpreparedness but did not impose harsher punishment. On June 13, 1861, Porterfield was replaced by Brigadier General Robert S. Garnett, who was later killed in action at Corrick's Ford on July 13, 1861, after a defeat at Rich Mountain on July 11. Porterfield joined General William W. Loring’s staff as chief of ordnance on August 9, 1861, and briefly commanded a brigade under General Edward "Allegheny" Johnson from April 21 to May 1, 1862. In May 1862, during the reorganization of the 25th Virginia Regiment, he was not re-elected to command. Feeling unfairly treated and denied promotion as recommended by Johnson, he resigned. He was captured by Union forces under General Nathaniel P. Banks in June or July 1862 but was soon paroled and never formally exchanged, taking no further part in the war. In 1871, Porterfield co-founded the Bank of Charles Town in Jefferson County, West Virginia, which he served as cashier for many years. He was a member of the Aztec Club of Mexican–American War veterans and, as one of the longest-lived and last three surviving members, served as vice president from 1914 to 1915 and president from 1915 to 1916. George A. Porterfield died on February 27, 1919, in Martinsburg, West Virginia, and was buried at Greenhill Cemetery in Martinsburg. At his death, he was the third-last surviving veteran officer of the Mexican–American War.
